Both species of seahorse native to the UK are protected by law. You may need a wildlife licence if you intend to carry out an activity that is likely to disturb seahorses or damage their habitat. Understand and apply for marine wildlife licences

Supporting seagrass recovery and restoration

Protecting existing seagrass and reducing the pressures that caused damage should be considered before restoration work begins. Depending on the site, this can include managing recreation, providing alternatives to anchoring, replacing traditional moorings, improving water quality and reducing impacts from development or fishing activity.

MMO’s role

MMO assesses and manages the effects of marine non licensable activities on marine protected areas within 12 nautical miles of the English coast. This includes sites where seagrass is a protected feature.

Consents and licences

Collecting seagrass or plants, depositing material, installing restoration equipment or carrying out other works may require a marine licence, wildlife licence or advice from Natural England.

It is an offence under section 140 of the Marine and Coastal Access Act 2009 to intentionally pick, collect, cut, uproot or destroy, any plant in a Marine Conservation Zone (MCZ) which is a protected feature of that MCZ. Natural England advise that anyone with plans to collect seagrass seeds or plants should liaise with Natural England on methods and suitable locations prior to this collection, to enable projects to progress swiftly without hindering recovery of designated seagrass beds and to avoid committing an offence.

Additionally, as a wild flowering plant, the removal or uprooting of seagrass plants is prohibited under Section 13(1)(b) under the Wildlife & Countryside Act 1981. Please seek advice from Natural England in this case.

MMO Marine Licence

It is your responsibility, as the applicant, to determine if you require a marine licence for activities in the marine environment: Find out if you need a marine licence and see our guidance on how to make a marine licence application for further information on the marine licensing process, timescales and any associated fees.

MMO Wildlife Licence

Section 9 of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 protects both species of seahorse native to the UK: spiny or long-snouted seahorse (Hippocampus guttulatus) and short snouted seahorse (Hippocampus hippocampus). You must have a wildlife licence if you are diving or snorkelling and intending to do something likely to disturb seahorses, or damage the habitat they live in. This could be diving in a known seahorse location, taking photographs, filming seahorses or removing seagrass.

Further advice on restoring seagrass:

Restoration Handbooks published to give best practice advice on creating new estuarine and coastal habitats

Seagrass Restoration Handbook - CaBA (catchmentbasedapproach.org)

ReMEDIES Seagrass Cultivation & Restoration Best Practice Guide

Seagrass restoration - best practice case studies

ReMEDIES

ReMEDIES stands for Reducing and Mitigating Erosion and Disturbance Impacts Effecting the Seabed.

The LIFE Recreation ReMEDIES project focused on how sensitive seabed habitats are impacted by recreational activities and provides a number of case studies which demonstrate how varied management measures can be effective. It aimed to reduce recreational pressure, restore seagrass habitats and promote awareness.

The project installed advance mooring systems (AMS) to protect the seagrass, and implemented Voluntary No Anchor Zones (VNAZ) to manage access to seagrass beds. The Royal Yachting Association (RYA) Green Blue Project advises best practice for recreational boating providing the Green Guide to Anchoring and Moorings to help minimise disturbance, and identifying UK seagrass bed locations to inform boaters of where to be more vigilant when considering an anchor spot.

Active restoration was key to the ReMEDIES project. The Ocean Conservation Trust planted a total of eight hectares of seagrass meadows within two Special Areas of Conservation (SAC).

Ocean Conservation Trust

The Ocean Conservation Trust exists to protect and restore the ocean. Their vision is a world where the ocean is thriving, healthy, and sustainably protected for generations to come. The Ocean Conservation Trust’s Blue Meadows project is a holistic approach to seagrass protection, regeneration and restoration at scale.

The goal is to protect the seagrass we already have, and over the longer-term restore the seagrass we have lost. ‘Blue Meadows’ places local communities at the heart of its work through community engagement, enabling coastal communities to feel inspired and empowered to help protect their local seagrass meadows and equipping them with the resources to do so.

The Ocean Conservation Trust have developed an immersive experience, so everyone can explore the wonders of seagrass, no matter their age or where they live.
